base-conversion.body:
`%u` is base 10 over `"0123456789"`. `%x` is base 16 over `"0123456789abcdef"`. `%X` is base 16
over `"0123456789ABCDEF"`. Everything else — accumulate the remainder, recurse or stack the digits
so they come out most-significant-first, stop when the quotient reaches zero, print a lone `"0"`
for the value zero rather than nothing — is identical across all three. `%p` runs through the same
routine again: base 16, lowercase, over a pointer's bit pattern instead of an integer's.

Writing three separate conversion functions instead of one parameterised by base and alphabet is
how `%x` gets fixed and `%X` quietly does not — the two drift apart, and drift like that is exactly
what a differential test against the real `printf` is built to catch.
defense: Why should `%x` and `%X` be the same function with one parameter changed?
base-conversion.title: `%u`, `%x` and `%X` are the same algorithm three times: divide-and-remainder against a base, indexed into a digit alphabet.

int-min.body:
`%d` and `%i` share one signed-decimal routine, and that routine's most tempting first line —
negate a negative argument so the digit-extraction loop only ever handles positives — is exactly
the line that overflows on `INT_MIN`. Two's complement is asymmetric: `INT_MIN` is `-2147483648`,
`INT_MAX` is only `2147483647`, so `+2147483648` has no representation as `int` and negating
`INT_MIN` is undefined behaviour, not merely a wrong number.

Three legitimate fixes exist: promote to `long` before negating; extract digits from the negative
value directly using `%` and `/`, both of which truncate toward zero and give the right digit
either way; or special-case the ten-digit literal for `INT_MIN`. Which one you chose matters less
than being able to say which, and why the naive line was wrong in the first place.
defense: Why does `%d` crash — or print the wrong thing — on `INT_MIN`?
int-min.title: `-(-2147483648)` does not fit back into an `int`.

no-buffering.body:
The real `printf` batches bytes into an internal buffer and flushes on a newline, on the buffer
filling, or on `fflush`/exit — none of that traffic reaches the descriptor as it happens. Subject
IV says plainly not to implement that buffer management, which means every `write` your conversions
perform has to land on the descriptor immediately, unbuffered, in exactly the order the format
string produced it.

This is what makes fd capture a meaningful oracle at all: a test asserting the exact byte sequence
on descriptor `1` only works if what reaches `write()` matches a byte-for-byte reading of the
format string, one conversion at a time. It is also why the closed-descriptor case in
`pf_robust` can observe correct output from the conversions that ran *before* the failing one —
nothing was ever held back waiting on a flush that this project is not allowed to have.
defense: What does 'do not implement the buffer management of the original printf()' actually forbid you from doing?
no-buffering.title: The subject forbids reimplementing `printf`'s buffer management, which changes what a test is even allowed to observe.

null-string-ub.body:
Passing `NULL` is not a documented edge case with a spec-mandated answer; it is outside what the
standard defines at all, which is a different thing from "unspecified" or "implementation-defined".
glibc chooses to print the seven characters `(null)` rather than let `strlen` dereference a NULL
pointer and crash — that is glibc being defensive, not glibc following a rule your `ft_printf` is
bound by.

The naive path — call `strlen`/`ft_strlen` on the argument before checking it — segfaults, and this
subject scores a crash as non-functional (Chapter II) even though the standard permits *any*
behaviour here, undefined behaviour included. So most implementations pick a printable fallback on
purpose, and the sentence worth having ready at defense names the behaviour as undefined and states
what yours does and why, not that there is one true output.
null-string-ub.title: `printf("%s", NULL)` has no behaviour the C standard defines — the standard requires `%s`'s argument to point at a string, full stop.

pointer-format.body:
`%p`'s argument is `void *`. Handing it to the base-conversion routine means first reinterpreting
its bits as an integer type wide enough to hold every one of them — that type is `uintptr_t`
(`<stdint.h>`), which the standard actually guarantees round-trips a pointer. `unsigned long`
happens to be wide enough on the platforms this project is graded on; code that says `uintptr_t`
states what it depends on, and code that says `unsigned long` is depending on an assumption it
never wrote down.

The NULL case is where this concept meets the subject head-on: `printf("%p", NULL)` is not
standardised, so "prepend `0x`, then convert" and "check for NULL first" produce different answers
on different platforms — glibc prints `(nil)`, macOS's libc prints `0x0`. Since Subject IV says
your function "will be compared against the original `printf()`", which of those two is *correct*
depends entirely on which platform is doing the comparing.
defense: Why does `%p` go through `uintptr_t` instead of `unsigned long`?
pointer-format.title: A pointer is not an integer, and printing one means reinterpreting its bit pattern, not its value in any arithmetic sense.

return-count.body:
Every byte that reaches `write` counts toward the return value — literal text between conversions,
the single byte `%%` produces, an unknown conversion your robustness branch chooses to echo
verbatim. The only design that keeps this reliably correct is one shared accumulator that every
branch adds to on its way out. A `%c` branch that returns early without touching that accumulator
is a bug that a suite testing `%c` alone will never see, because it only shows up once `%c` shares
a format string with something else.

This is also why the contract for this pack asserts the return count on *every* case, not only in
`pf_ret`: it is not one suite's property, it is the one number every suite is jointly responsible
for.
defense: Does `ft_printf(\"%s%d\", \"ab\", 3)` count the `3` even though neither conversion is in `pf_ret`?
return-count.title: The number ft_printf returns is a running total accumulated across the whole call, not a length computed after the fact.

unsigned-reinterpret.body:
The argument promotes to `int` the same way regardless of which conversion reads it; what changes
is the type `va_arg` names when fetching it. Fetch it as `unsigned int` and a negative bit pattern
is simply read differently — no arithmetic happens, no sign is inspected. `-1` as a 32-bit `int` is
the bit pattern `0xFFFFFFFF`; as `unsigned int` that same bit pattern is `4294967295`.

```
-1 as int              = 0xFFFFFFFF
same bits as unsigned  = 4294967295      ← what %u must print
abs(-1)                = 1               ← a different routine, wrong answer
```

Reinterpretation is free the moment the local variable is declared `unsigned int` — the mistake is
doing work you were not asked to do, by calling `abs()` or hand-flipping the sign before
conversion. That produces `1`, four billion away from the answer the original `printf` gives.
defense: What does `%u` print for the argument `-1`, and why is it not `1`?
unsigned-reinterpret.title: `%u` and `%x` do not convert a negative number into a positive one — they read the same bits under a different type.

va-copy.body:
Once `va_start(ap, format)` runs, `ap` is a live, one-directional cursor: every `va_arg(ap, T)`
advances it by the width of `T`, permanently. Passing `ap` itself into a helper function does not
reliably hand that helper an independent copy — on the x86-64 System V ABI, `va_list` is an
array type, so a "by value" parameter decays to a pointer, and the helper's reads move the
caller's cursor too. On another ABI the same code might genuinely copy the state and never fail a
single test, which is exactly what makes this bug invisible until it meets the wrong platform.

`va_copy(dst, src)` is the only portable way to get a second, independent cursor over the
arguments `src` has not yet consumed. Every `va_copy` needs its own `va_end`, same as the original
`va_start` does — copying it does not exempt it from being closed.
defense: What goes wrong if you pass a `va_list` to a helper by value and then keep reading it in the caller?
va-copy.title: A `va_list` is a single cursor into the argument frame; reading it moves it, and there is no way to move it back.

variadic-promotion.body:
C99 §6.5.2.2 requires the *default argument promotions* on every trailing argument of a variadic
call, before the call even happens. The caller's `ft_printf("%c", 'A')` does not push a one-byte
`'A'` — the compiler has already promoted it to an `int`-sized slot by the time your function sees
the argument list. `va_arg` only knows how to read the promoted type; there is no macro for reading
a narrower one, because the narrower one was never actually written.

```
va_arg(ap, char)   → wrong: reads the wrong width off a list built with int-sized slots
va_arg(ap, int)    → correct; narrow afterward with (unsigned char)va_arg(ap, int)
```

`%c` is the one conversion in this subject where the mismatch is visible immediately — `%d`, `%u`,
`%x` and `%X` all already declare `int`/`unsigned int`, which is the promoted type anyway, so the
bug hides behind them. It does not hide behind `%c`.
defense: Why must `va_arg(ap, char)` never appear in your ft_printf?
variadic-promotion.title: `char` and `short` never travel through `...` at their own size; they arrive already widened to `int`, and `float` arrives as `double`.

write-partial.body:
`ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count)` returns the number of bytes it actually
wrote, which can be less than `count` — a full pipe, a signal, a closed descriptor — and can be
`-1` on error, with nothing written at all. An accumulator that adds `count` unconditionally,
instead of adding whatever `write` actually returned, reports bytes that were never sent the
moment a single call comes back short.

The subject's robustness case for this is a closed file descriptor: `write` returns `-1`, your
return value has to go negative to reflect it, and the conversions that already ran before the
failing `write` keep whatever they already produced — nothing may crash trying to keep converting
past it.
defense: Your ft_printf writes to a closed file descriptor. What has to happen?
write-partial.title: `write` is a system call, not a library promise — it reports what happened, and what happened is not always all of it.

defense.answer: Default argument promotion widens every `char`, `short` or `float` argument before it is placed in the variable argument list — `char` arrives as `int`, `float` arrives as `double`. `va_arg(ap, char)` reads the wrong width off a list that was built with `int`-sized slots; the fix is `va_arg(ap, int)` followed by a cast down to the byte you actually want.
defense.question: Why must `va_arg(ap, char)` never appear in your ft_printf?

defense.answer: On some ABIs (x86-64 System V) `va_list` is really an array, so a "by value" parameter decays to a pointer and the helper's reads move the caller's cursor too — the caller then reads whatever argument the helper already consumed. On another ABI the same code might genuinely copy the state and never fail, which is what makes the bug invisible until it meets the wrong platform. `va_copy` is the portable fix.
defense.question: What goes wrong if you pass a `va_list` to a helper by value and then keep reading it in the caller?

defense.answer: `4294967295`. `-1` as a 32-bit `int` is the bit pattern `0xFFFFFFFF`; `%u` reinterprets those same bits as `unsigned int` instead of converting the value, so it prints `2^32 - 1`. `abs(-1)` gives `1`, which is a different routine solving a different problem.
defense.question: What does `%u` print for the argument `-1`?

defense.answer: Both are base-16 division-and-remainder against the same accumulator logic; the only real difference is which sixteen-character alphabet the remainder indexes into. Two independent functions means every future fix has to be made twice, and the two conversions drifting apart is exactly what a differential test against the real `printf` is built to catch.
defense.question: Why should `%x` and `%X` be the same function with one parameter changed?

defense.answer: `uintptr_t` is the type `<stdint.h>` actually guarantees can hold a pointer's bit pattern and round-trip it. `unsigned long` happens to be wide enough on the platforms this project is graded on, but code that says `uintptr_t` states exactly what it depends on, and code that says `unsigned long` is depending on an assumption it never wrote down.
defense.question: Why does `%p` go through `uintptr_t` instead of `unsigned long`?

defense.answer: There is no single correct answer — it is platform-defined. glibc prints `(nil)`; macOS's libc prints `0x0`. Since the subject compares your output against "the original `printf()`", the right answer depends on which platform is doing the comparing, and the honest thing to say at defense is which one you targeted and why, not that there is one true output.
defense.question: What should `ft_printf("%p", NULL)` print?

defense.answer: Yes — the return value is a running total across the whole call, not something specific to a "return count" suite. `"ab"` contributes 2, `"3"` contributes 1, the total is 3. Any branch that produces bytes without touching the shared accumulator is wrong the moment it shares a format string with something else, even if its own suite passes in isolation.
defense.question: Does `ft_printf("%s%d", "ab", 3)` count the `3` in its return value, even though neither conversion is `pf_ret`?

defense.answer: `write` returns `-1` and sets `errno`; your return value must reflect that failure by going negative, and nothing may crash or keep converting the rest of the format string as though the write had succeeded. The bug this catches is an accumulator that adds what you *asked* `write` to send instead of what `write` says it actually sent.
defense.question: Your ft_printf writes to a closed file descriptor. What has to happen?

defense.answer: `INT_MIN` is `-2147483648`; its positive counterpart, `2147483648`, does not exist as an `int`, since the range tops out at `2147483647`. A routine that negates the argument first to make it positive invokes undefined behaviour on exactly this value. I avoid the negation entirely by <promoting to `long` / extracting digits from the negative value with `%` and `/` / special-casing it>.
defense.question: Why does `%d` crash — or print the wrong thing — on `INT_MIN`?

defense.answer: No. The C standard requires `%s`'s argument to point at a valid string; `NULL` is outside what it defines at all. glibc prints `(null)` instead of crashing, which is glibc's own defensive choice, not a rule I am bound by. The answer worth giving names it as undefined and states what my implementation does.
defense.question: Is `printf("%s", NULL)` defined behaviour?

defense.answer: It forbids accumulating output in an internal buffer and flushing it in batches the way `printf` does. Every byte a conversion produces has to reach `write` as that conversion runs, in format-string order — which is also the only reason a test can assert an exact byte sequence on a descriptor at all, and the only reason correct output before a failing `write` stays visible.
defense.question: The subject says "do not implement the buffer management of the original printf()." What does that forbid?

defense.answer: Each `va_arg` call has to advance the shared cursor by exactly the promoted width of the type it names, exactly once per argument the format string actually consumes — an unknown specifier that still consumes an argument, or a known one that gets skipped, desynchronises every conversion after it. Anything that needs to look at an argument without permanently consuming it needs `va_copy`, not a `va_list` passed around by value.
defense.question: Two format specifiers in one call each need to read the argument list. What has to stay true between them?
